speaker: Alex
text: Wait, so when an agent moves through a door, it isn’t merely changing a label on a map?

speaker: Sam
text: No—the movement is grounded in WorldGraph, the runtime source of truth. Typed nodes sit in an ID-keyed dictionary, while directed, typed relationships sit in a list.

speaker: Alex
text: And that graph is not a frozen snapshot. You can add, remove, query, filter, serialize, load, and update it during play?

speaker: Sam
text: Right. Areas, ways, items, characters, and triggers can change while the world keeps running.

speaker: Alex
text: So what began as a Flask backend with a modular JavaScript browser client became a simulation we can inspect from several angles?

speaker: Sam
text: Basically. Documented subsystems now cover shared actors, LLM and memory services, time modes, survival, combat, world geography, items, narration, scenario editing, and observability.

speaker: Alex
text: The part I keep coming back to is that boundary: the graph stores the world, while other services reason over it and present it.

speaker: Sam
text: Exactly. Today we trace the architecture and what comes next.

speaker: Alex
text: I want to push back on the chatbot label. It can produce convincing prose, but VirtualWorld must remember what is true between turns and rules.

speaker: Sam
text: Exactly. VirtualWorld is a text-based simulation engine for AI beings: a Flask backend and modular JavaScript browser client.

speaker: Alex
text: WorldGraph is the runtime source of truth, not a separate database or abstract model. If absent, it does not exist in the world.

speaker: Sam
text: Typed nodes sit in an ID-keyed dictionary. Directed, typed relationships sit in a list.

speaker: Alex
text: An area and the way out of it differ. One relationship joins them.

speaker: Sam
text: Not a room list with adjectives. Areas, ways, items, characters, triggers, and their links are inspectable shared world state.

speaker: Alex
text: WorldGraph is active, not decorative. The engine can add, remove, query, filter, serialize, load, and update during play.

speaker: Sam
text: That differs from “the AI is narrating.” Movement reads connections, triggers change properties, serialization writes the graph.

speaker: Alex
text: Saving makes the boundary obvious. The graph gets serialized, and loading reconstructs the world from it.

speaker: Sam
text: Runtime JSON makes that explicit. Under “graph,” ID-keyed nodes carry type, name, and properties; edges carry source, target, and type.

speaker: Alex
text: That state must line up across the backend, browser client, rules, and save file. Otherwise narration could look coherent while the simulation underneath it disagrees.

speaker: Sam
text: That mismatch is why this is more than a conversation wrapper. The graph gives the services one thing to agree on.

speaker: Alex
text: Think not “characters talking somewhere fictional,” but “agents reading and changing shared world state.”

speaker: Sam
text: That makes debugging concrete. What does the engine know, where does it live, and which relationship or property caused the next event?

speaker: Alex
text: Space is relational, not metric. Connections define the theater; there are no distances to calculate.

speaker: Sam
text: Right. The graph is not storage underneath the experience; it is the playable world. Next, let's follow one action from the browser to the backend and watch it change.

speaker: Alex
text: Let’s follow one command through actor selection, action handling, world effects, and time. The action is only the entrance to the cycle.

speaker: Sam
text: The browser sends it; the backend resolves who acts and updates shared state. The command is one event in a larger engine transaction.

speaker: Alex
text: VirtualWorld supports continuous, sequential, random, and d20 modes. Continuous acts immediately; the others use a queue to select the next actor.

speaker: Sam
text: The queue reconciles living players into alphabetical sequential order, reshuffled random order, or d20-plus-DEX initiative. The selected player submits the command; the backend then applies it.

speaker: Alex
text: After the action, sequential, random, or d20 control passes to the next actor. Continuous play has no queue slot, but it still follows the same engine world-processing rule.

speaker: Sam
text: Here’s the bit I used to blur: every player action triggers the full tick_turn cycle, including continuous play. The command must not cause a second pass.

speaker: Alex
text: tick_turn processes conditions, decays vitals, applies environmental effects, drifts temperature, ticks items, processes NPCs, and advances the clock once.

speaker: Sam
text: Those are consequences of the action, even when the player sees narration. One call means one system pass and one decay application, not another during rendering.

speaker: Alex
text: The clock detail is easy to misstate. The engine defaults to one minute per tick; the referenced world_template.json scenario sets five minutes per turn.

speaker: Sam
text: That is configuration: one tick is one minute or five scenario minutes. The same action can advance different amounts of game time.

speaker: Alex
text: Completing a sequential, random, or d20 queue cycle increments turn_number, advances the world clock, and applies tick and decay effects exactly once.

speaker: Sam
text: tick_turn processes before turn_number changes, and clearing events opens the next turn. Cleanup must never become a second execution path.

speaker: Alex
text: So the command says what happened, coordination says who acts, and tick_turn says how the world responds. Next, we’ll open the cycle and inspect every boundary where something might fire twice.

speaker: Sam
text: Before we hunt for double-firing boundaries, there’s a bigger simplification hiding in plain sight: a soak NPC, a simple NPC, an LLM agent, and the human player all use the same Player model.

speaker: Alex
text: Exactly. They read and write the same world state, submit the same actions, and advance on the same clock. What changes is the decision controller—and what that choice costs.

speaker: Sam
text: A soak character can use a deterministic survival policy; a simple NPC can follow scheduled or scripted behavior; an LLM agent can choose with a model; a human chooses through the interface.

speaker: Alex
text: So “autonomy” is not a different kind of physics. It is a decision loop attached to the controls every character already has.

speaker: Sam
text: That keeps the comparison honest. If an LLM agent can use a capability the cheap policy cannot, the world’s rules depend on who is paying attention, which is a very expensive form of drama.

speaker: Alex
text: Cognition should refine the next action, not invent a new one. The shared action system remains the boundary of what anybody can actually do.

speaker: Sam
text: And the human case has one hard guardrail: the engine may execute a human’s chosen action, but it must never act autonomously for the human.

speaker: Alex
text: BackgroundSimulation.process_due is the shared executor, skipping only the human’s own character, and only because the human is the decision source.

speaker: Sam
text: I like “only because.” It prevents a convenience from quietly becoming player control.

speaker: Alex
text: The LLM path uses an OpenAI-compatible interface, so it can support multiple providers, endpoints, and models. Token limits, rate limits, streaming, and logging manage the decision path without changing the world’s action set.

speaker: Sam
text: Structured memory consolidates state for reasoning, reflection, editing, and tools. It can improve the next choice, but it cannot bypass the shared action schema.

speaker: Alex
text: Next, we’ll put deterministic, scripted, model-driven, and human controllers behind one choice. Then we can compare loops without changing the game underneath.

speaker: Alex
text: The shared action set has a spatial consequence: no coordinates. A character uses one typed graph-edge anchor relative to a room entity: at, on, under, behind, or beside.

speaker: Sam
text: “Jake at the piano” is therefore world state, not decorative phrasing. A new position clears the previous anchor, so Jake cannot be beside the piano and trapped under the chandelier at once.

speaker: Alex
text: The core rule is automatic: a physical action walks you there. Opening or closing a way puts you at it, and using an item on that way does the same.

speaker: Sam
text: Giving, stealing, grabbing, or attacking someone puts you beside that target. Using an item on a room object can put you at, on, or under it from tags and phrasing.

speaker: Alex
text: Movement carries that rule through the way and into the destination room. The position edge records where the action actually put you, so the graph can represent meaningful proximity.

speaker: Sam
text: That also means no ceremonial “examine it first” step. If an action physically involves the piano, the graph already reflects that you reached the piano.

speaker: Alex
text: Items use the same principle. An item in a room has an in edge from the item to the room; an item held by a player has a carrying edge to that player.

speaker: Sam
text: Take the rusty key and the engine removes its in edge to the room, then adds a carrying edge to the traveler. Drop it, and those moves reverse.

speaker: Alex
text: The source is the thing being positioned; the target is its room, surface, container, or owner. That consistent direction makes the resulting world state inspectable.

speaker: Sam
text: There is a legacy Player.inventory property, which sounds suspiciously like an inventory array. Engine inventory operations do not consult it; the graph edge is authoritative.

speaker: Alex
text: Because carried items point to players, they can be excluded from room-item queries. No second bag needs to be synchronized, repaired, or left stale.

speaker: Sam
text: Next, these edges feed the shared action loop. No controller gets any special powers.

speaker: Alex
text: That shared loop becomes visible through temperature. A room defaults to 21°C, while a character’s core Temperature vital starts at 37°C; one is ambient, the other bodily.

speaker: Sam
text: Before the body drifts, worn insulation and weather produce effective temperature: ambient plus insulation, wind chill, and humidity modifier. Two characters sharing that room can feel quite different because of those modifiers.

speaker: Alex
text: Every tick uses effective temperature, not the room reading. Below 5°C, core temperature falls by 0.02 times the gap from 5°C; above 35°C, it rises by 0.02 times the gap above 35°C.

speaker: Sam
text: But the comfort range isn’t immunity. Between 5°C and 35°C, the body self-regulates toward 37°C by 0.1°C per tick; insulation still matters once effective temperature crosses a threshold.

speaker: Alex
text: Drift is only the first consequence. At 35.0–36.9°C, Energy drops by one from shivering; at 33.0–34.9°C, Energy -2 and HP -1; below 33°C, HP -3 per tick.

speaker: Sam
text: Heat works in parallel: 37.1–38.0°C costs one Thirst, 38.1–40.0°C costs one HP, and above 40°C costs three HP per tick. Damage uses the new core temperature after drift.

speaker: Alex
text: Below 30°C, death is attributed to hypothermia; above 42°C, it is heat stroke. Even before either threshold, HP regeneration is blocked outside 35–39°C, so temperature gates recovery.

speaker: Sam
text: The interface keeps the actual Celsius value. The core-temperature vital maps 25–45°C to 0–100%, appends a °C suffix, and changes from blue and green through yellow to red.

speaker: Alex
text: The color shows the vital’s position, while prose explains the experience. Descriptions and warnings use effective feels-like temperature after insulation: “Pleasant” starts at 18°C; “Freezing” starts at -10°C. At 35°C, the warning explicitly says, “You’re overheating; find shade or water.”

speaker: Sam
text: That separation matters: the 21°C room remains the raw source reading while clothing, wind, and humidity alter that pressure. The narration reacts to experienced temperature; the bar tracks physiological danger.

speaker: Alex
text: Next, we can make it actionable. Conditions can fire when temperature gets too low or high, while effects push the environment back toward safety.

speaker: Alex
text: Temperature tells us when a room is unsafe, not what belongs in it. Start with a blank scenario and build its runtime graph first.

speaker: Sam
text: The graph is the runtime source of truth. Nodes use id, type, name, and properties for area, way, item, character, and trigger; typed edges hold relationships.

speaker: Alex
text: Every interactive thing should be a node, and every relationship an edge. Flexibility does not remove conventions: required properties still need deliberate authoring.

speaker: Sam
text: Character state is separate: top-level players is authoritative for personality, vitals, skills, memories, emotion, autonomy, and behavior. Top-level world_lore is injected into every agent prompt.

speaker: Alex
text: Serialized areas, rooms, ways, item_registry, and players_in_area are convenience views, not alternatives. If one disagrees with the graph, the runtime follows the graph.

speaker: Sam
text: The persistent library lives under data/library/. It stores one JSON file per entry in type-specific directories: items, tags, areas, characters, conditions, triggers, behaviours, or structures.

speaker: Alex
text: That makes this a two-stage contract: author the graph first, then create reusable entries without another source of truth. Population should extend the scenario, not quietly rewrite it.

speaker: Sam
text: Tags are case-insensitive classifiers, stored as lists or comma strings. Because tag files are id-keyed, saving an existing id is an upsert, so repeats deduplicate.

speaker: Alex
text: The auto-furnishing chain is stricter than ordinary tag lookup. An area’s domain tag must also appear in the furniture item’s domain tags and in at least one placeable item’s domain tags.

speaker: Sam
text: That is plain set intersection across all three levels, not a vague “library-ish” match. Wooden and other descriptive tags, or setting tags like interior, cannot stand in for the domain match.

speaker: Alex
text: Furniture roles then select the valid placement targets: display uses on or beside; container and storage use in; floors use at. The role supplies the spatial grammar rather than just a catalogue label.

speaker: Sam
text: Together, domain and role prevent a generated room from putting books on rugs merely because both appeared nearby. Next, we’ll follow one blank area through authoring, population, and placement.

speaker: Alex
text: Now that the blank area is authored, populated, and furnished, strange runtime behavior calls for a more disciplined debugging pass. Inspect the selected entity before rewriting JSON by intuition.

speaker: Sam
text: The Inspector is context-sensitive across areas, items, ways, characters, memories, behaviours, and lore. It uses a singleton architecture, with window.inspector coordinating specialized views.

speaker: Alex
text: Rendering has one strict owner: panel.js is the only file that writes to #inspector-panel, while the views render through centralized lit-html output. That avoids mixing direct DOM writes with lit's part tracking.

speaker: Sam
text: So start with the entity, its graph edges, conditions, and behaviours. If several entities share the same odd behavior, the problem may sit below the authored content.

speaker: Alex
text: That is where Engine Config enters. Through /api/settings/engine_config, it exposes tunables such as sound penetration, heat propagation, and light spill.

speaker: Sam
text: Defaults can be overridden in data/engine_config.json, and a saved value takes effect on the next engine call. You no longer need to edit Python or restart the server to test a constant.

speaker: Alex
text: The interface is schema-driven, and Apply rerenders from the server-coerced response, so the fields show what actually persisted. Reset to defaults restores the built-ins without pretending an unsaved edit is live.

speaker: Sam
text: After inspection and tuning, we need a record of what the player actually saw. WorldExport.exportEventLog writes the visible event stream to Markdown for a clean runtime trace.

speaker: Alex
text: The export distinguishes two clocks: Tick N is the global event-sequence id used for ordering and the filename. Turn N with HH:MM is the separate in-game world turn.

speaker: Sam
text: It exports only the visible stream, so filtered hidden logs, including disabled LLM logs, stay out. That makes the artifact evidence of the interface, not a dump of internal records.

speaker: Alex
text: Together, those layers create a useful loop: inspect the entity, tune only what is genuinely systemic, reproduce the issue, then export the exact visible trace. Next, we can follow one suspicious event through that loop and see where those two layers actually disagree.

speaker: Alex
text: Library 2.0 makes every library save round-trip every field. Full-schema editors replace tab-specific guesswork, and validate and coerce hooks warn on unknown keys and missing required values.

speaker: Sam
text: That stops the quiet failure where a successful-looking save drops part of an entry. Synchronization can also overwrite good live data with a stale library copy.

speaker: Alex
text: The safer path backs up the existing file, guards the write, and verifies the replacement before accepting it. An incomplete or unreadable result is rejected rather than silently taking the entry’s place. A loud failure is inconvenient; a silent one can erase authored work.

speaker: Sam
text: That is where DiffModal earns its keep. Instead of automatically clobbering a category, it resolves per-entry conflicts for memories, items, relationships, conditions, vitals, decay rates, and equipped slots.

speaker: Alex
text: It shows change counts, status badges, old-versus-new values, and select-all controls. You choose entries in either direction, while whole-category clobbering remains available when wholesale replacement is intentional.

speaker: Sam
text: I’d keep that option, but never as the default. “Replace everything” should look as consequential as it is.

speaker: Alex
text: Scenario storage makes the same distinctions. data/autosave.json is the live copy; saves/<name>_<timestamp>.json stores a manual full-state save with scenario, tick, turn, player, version, and autosave metadata.

speaker: Sam
text: Meanwhile, data/scenarios/<name>.json remains the authored source. Live autosave edits never flow back into source JSON, and Restart reloads the source instead of saving the live copy over it.

speaker: Alex
text: Restart can discard uncommitted runtime changes, but it cannot masquerade as committing them. Moving live edits into the source requires an explicit commit, not a casual Save label.

speaker: Sam
text: So the workflow has three promises: autosave preserves the current run, manual save stores a named state, and commit updates the authored scenario. Confusing them is how people lose work quietly.

speaker: Alex
text: The save path should show what changed, protect what was good, and stop when new data cannot be trusted. Next, we can try breaking it with a messy character under real editing pressure and see whether those safeguards hold.

speaker: Alex
text: The biggest idea is that VirtualWorld is not a chatbot wearing a world costume. It is a world model with a deliberate contract: the graph is shared truth, every action advances the simulation, and people and agents operate through the same player controls. Lose track of that, and better prose becomes prettier improvisation.

speaker: Sam
text: The save workflow has to honor the same contract. Autosave protects the run, manual save stores a named state, and only an explicit commit changes the authored scenario. That separation may feel bureaucratic until the first bad overwrite teaches the hard lesson.

speaker: Alex
text: Next, I’d build the messy-character stress test: edit one entity while its relationships, inventory, and survival state are in motion, then force a conflicting change. I want to see whether the diff, backup, and guarded write explain themselves under pressure.

speaker: Sam
text: And if they fail, I want them to fail dramatically enough that we notice.

speaker: Alex
text: That is our highest standard for debugging.

speaker: Sam
text: Thanks for building this with me. I’m excited to keep pushing.
